# Democracy experiment {#sec-gs}

@graham2020democracy ask whether voters punish candidates who violate democratic principles when
party and policy favor them. Respondents chose between two hypothetical state legislative
candidates in up to thirteen matchups. The candidates differed in party, economic and social
policy, governance practices, democratic violations, scandals, and personal traits. This chapter
reproduces the paper's results and figures from the saved fit.

```{r}
#| label: gs-setup
#| cache: false
library(sconjoint)
fits <- getOption("sconjoint.fits", "fits")
gs <- sc_load(file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
if (is.null(gs)) stop("This chapter needs the saved fit gs_q3.rds; see the installation chapter.")
# a short table of estimates
tab <- function(e, digits = 3) {
  out <- e[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "se", "lower", "upper", "n")]
  out[2:6] <- lapply(out[2:6], round, digits)
  out
}
```

```{r}
#| label: gs-knitr
#| include: false
#| cache: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(pointsize = 11))
```

The book's file `_figs-helpers.R` holds the paper's plotting code. Its `estimate_each()` runs
independent targets in parallel, with the same results as one `sc_estimate()` call.

```{r}
#| label: gs-helpers
#| cache: false
#| file: _figs-helpers.R
```

## Data and fit

`sc_example_data("gs")` builds the paper's inputs from the bundled `gs2020` data: 1,605
respondents, 20,657 matchups, and 30 coded features. `y = 1` means the left candidate was chosen.
The network uses sixteen respondent characteristics measured before the tasks. The data also carry
the paper's five folds, the early-stopping respondents of each fold, and the grouping variables.

```{r}
#| label: gs-data
x <- sc_example_data("gs")
x
head(x$groups)
```

The groups are party ID (`pid7`, from -3 strong Democrat to 3 strong Republican), party (`party`,
leaners counted as partisans), self-described ideology (`ideology`, all respondents), and `PL`,
which is 1 for the 1,377 partisans and leaners. The co-partisan feature is always zero for the 228
pure independents, so their choices carry no information on that taste. Quantities about party
therefore use `w = "PL"`.

The paper fitted one to four taste factors and chose three. The code below reproduces the saved
fit with the defaults of `sc_fit()` and `sc_states()`, which are the paper's settings. It takes
several hours and is not run here.

```{r}
#| label: gs-fit
#| eval: false
fit_q <- lapply(1:4, function(q) sc_fit(x, q = q))   # five folds at each rank
sc_select_rank(fit_q)
gs <- sc_states(fit_q[[3]])                           # q = 3; M = 300 designs, 4 responses each
sc_save(gs, file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
```

`sc_select_rank()` gives the paper's rank table:

| Taste factors | Held-out log score | Gain over $q - 1$ | Paired $z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | -7.797 | | |
| 2 | -7.772 | 0.0249 | 2.19 |
| 3 (selected) | -7.739 | 0.0329 | 2.99 |
| 4 | -7.742 | -0.0029 | -0.47 |

The log score is the average log probability of a held-out respondent's whole sequence of choices.
The rule stops at $q = 3$ because the fourth factor does not improve the fit.

## Mean tastes

`sc_mean()` estimates the average utility from one coded feature, on the logit scale. The
co-partisan mean averages over partisans and leaners, the others over all respondents. The figures
use the paper's short feature names.

```{r}
#| label: gs-means
fn <- gs$data$data$feature_names
w_of <- function(f) if (f == "diff_respParty") "PL" else NULL
means <- sc_estimate(gs, lapply(fn, function(f) sc_mean(f, f, w = w_of(f))))
labels <- c("Co-partisan", "Economic policy (+1)", "Social policy (+1)",
            "Committee structure", "Legislative staffing", "Legislative procedure",
            "Program evaluation", "Record-keeping", "Legislative schedule",
            "Ban protests", "Ignore courts", "Executive orders", "Gerrymander (2 seats)",
            "Gerrymander (10 seats)", "Prosecute journalists", "Close polling stations",
            "Extramarital affair", "Underpaid taxes", "Female", "Asian", "Black", "Hispanic",
            "Farmer", "Lawyer", "Legislative staffer", "Police officer", "Army veteran",
            "Navy veteran", "Small business owner", "Teacher")
tab(means[c(1:3, 10:18), ])
```

Among partisans and leaners, a co-partisan candidate gains 0.81 units of utility on average. Each
step toward the conservative end of economic policy costs 0.24. The seven undemocratic actions
(`u_`) have negative means, from -0.53 (two-seat gerrymander) to -0.90 (prosecuting journalists).
The two scandals (`v_`) cost -0.94 (an affair) and -1.18 (underpaid taxes). Conduct is measured
against the generic reference position, a candidate who supports an elected oversight board.
`plug_in` is the cross-fitted value before the score correction (@sec-inference).

## Preference shares

`sc_share()` estimates the share of respondents with a positive taste for a contrast, averaging
over each respondent's fitted normal law. The paper's main figure reports shares for party, the two
policy scales, the seven violations and the two scandals. Each share needs its own bounded update
(about 15 seconds), so they run in parallel.

```{r}
#| label: gs-shares
fig_features <- fn[c(1:3, 10:18)]
shares <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(fig_features, function(f) sc_share(f, f, w = w_of(f))))
tab(shares, 4)
```

An estimated 82.5% of partisans and leaners prefer a co-partisan (95% interval 79.7% to 84.9%).
Shares favoring a violation are near zero and imprecise, 7.3% for closing polling stations
(interval 2.0% to 23.4%) and 0.2% for prosecuting journalists (interval 0 to 1). Such a share
depends on the spread of the taste across respondents. Each respondent saw each violation only
once, so that spread is measured imprecisely.

## Fitted distributions

`sc_fitted_law()` gives each held-out respondent's normal law of a taste, with the fitted mean and
the spread implied by the taste factors. The population law is their mixture.

```{r}
#| label: gs-laws
laws <- lapply(fn, function(f) sc_fitted_law(gs, f, w = w_of(f)))
attr(laws[[1]], "summary")
head(laws[[1]])
```

The two figures draw all 30 laws, as in the paper's appendix. The co-partisan curve lies mostly
right of zero and is wide. Most partisans prefer a co-partisan, by different amounts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-distributions-1
#| fig-cap: "Fitted tastes: party, policy and governance"
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 9.2
paper_par()
par(mfrow = c(5, 3), mar = c(1.7, .5, 1.9, .3), oma = c(1, .2, .2, .2))
for (j in 1:15) small_density(laws[[j]], labels[j], pick(means, fn[j]))
mtext("Utility contrast (logit units)", 1, outer = TRUE, line = .1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-distributions-2
#| fig-cap: "Fitted tastes: conduct and background"
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 9.2
paper_par()
par(mfrow = c(5, 3), mar = c(1.7, .5, 1.9, .3), oma = c(1, .2, .2, .2))
for (j in 16:30) small_density(laws[[j]], labels[j], pick(means, fn[j]))
mtext("Utility contrast (logit units)", 1, outer = TRUE, line = .1)
```

Blue curves are fitted values before the score correction. The red line and bar are the
score-corrected mean and its 95% interval, so the line need not sit at the curve's center. Each
panel has its own horizontal range and height. The co-partisan panel uses the 1,377
partisans and leaners, the others all 1,605 respondents. Policy is a one-point move toward the
conservative end. Conduct is compared with the generic reference position, sex with male, race with
white, and profession with business executive.

## Effects on choices

`sc_ame_switch()` gives the average marginal effect (AME) of switching one attribute of a
candidate, the model's counterpart of the AMCE (@sec-quantities). It takes the raw design
attribute, the level and the reference level. For party, the level is the respondent's own party
(1 = Democrat, 2 = Republican in the raw design) and the reference is the other party, so the
switch is undefined for pure independents. A policy AME switches from position 1 to position 4 and
divides by three, so it is per point of the scale. A conduct AME switches from the generic
reference position (`g_boardElect`) to the named violation.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ames
ame_target <- function(f) {
  if (f == "diff_respParty") {
    sc_ame_switch(f, "party",
                  level = function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                  ref = function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                  design = "gs", w = "PL")
  } else if (f %in% c("diff_p1_num", "diff_p2_num")) {
    sc_ame_switch(f, sub("^diff_(p[12])_num$", "\\1", f), 4L, 1L, design = "gs", scale = 1 / 3)
  } else {
    sc_ame_switch(f, "dem", f, "g_boardElect", design = "gs")
  }
}
ames <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(fig_features, ame_target))
tab(ames)
```

The regression AMCEs are the coefficients of a linear regression of the choice on all 30 coded
differences, among all respondents (partisans and leaners for party).

```{r}
#| label: gs-amce
dat <- gs$data$data                                    # y: choices; d: coded differences
partisan_rows <- rep(gs$data$groups$PL, dat$T) > 0
amce_all <- coef(lm(dat$y ~ dat$d))[-1]
amce_pl <- coef(lm(dat$y[partisan_rows] ~ dat$d[partisan_rows, ]))[-1]
amce <- setNames(c(amce_pl[1], amce_all[-1]), fn)
round(100 * amce[fig_features], 1)
```

A co-partisan candidate gains 14.0 percentage points of support, and a candidate who prosecutes
journalists loses 16.2 points. The regression AMCEs are 14.1 and -16.1 points.

The paper's main figure shows four views of each feature: the mean taste (A), its fitted
distribution (B), the share with a positive taste (C), and the AME with the regression AMCE as a
grey diamond (D).

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-preferences
#| fig-cap: "Preferences and choice effects"
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 5.5
jj <- match(fig_features, fn); yy <- rev(seq_along(jj))
paper_par()
layout(matrix(1:5, 1), widths = c(2.3, 1.45, 1.65, 1.6, 1.75))
row_labels(labels[jj])
panel(c(-1.55, 1.05), 12, "A. Mean\nutility", c(-1, 0, 1))
ci(pick(means, fig_features), yy)
panel(c(-4, 4), 12, "B. Fitted\npart-worths", c(-4, 0, 4))
for (j in seq_along(jj)) ridge(laws[[jj[j]]], yy[j], c(-4, 4))
panel(c(0, 100), 12, "C. Share\nfavoring (%)", c(0, 50, 100))
ci(pick(shares, fig_features), yy, scale = 100, hide_wide = TRUE)
panel(c(-26, 17), 12, "D. Choice\neffect (pp)", c(-20, 0, 15))
ci(pick(ames, fig_features), yy + .09, scale = 100)
points(100 * amce[fig_features], yy - .13, pch = 18, col = "#555555", cex = .85)
```

Panel B's curves are fitted values before the score correction, scaled to the same height, so
their centers need not match Panel A. In Panel C, a hollow point marks a share whose interval spans
at least 95 percentage points, and that interval is not drawn. Party uses partisans and leaners,
the other rows all respondents.

## Compensation shares

The *compensation share* is the share of respondents who prefer a co-partisan with a violation to
an otherwise identical non-co-partisan at the generic reference position. In `sc_share()` the
contrast is the sum of the two features. The paper computes it for the seven violations among
liberal, moderate and conservative partisans and leaners, 21 bounded updates in all.

```{r}
#| label: gs-comp
g <- gs$data$groups
violations <- grep("^diff_dem_code_u_", fn, value = TRUE)
comp <- list()
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) for (f in violations)
  comp[[length(comp) + 1]] <- sc_share(paste(ideo, f, sep = "."), c(f, "diff_respParty"),
                                       w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL)
comp_est <- estimate_each(gs, comp)
tab(comp_est[grepl("journalists", comp_est$name), ])
```

An estimated 33.8% of liberal partisans and leaners and 59.6% of conservative ones prefer the
co-partisan who prosecutes journalists, despite the large mean penalty of the violation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-compensation
#| fig-cap: "Compensation shares"
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
paper_par()
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 3), 2, byrow = TRUE), widths = c(2.2, 5), heights = c(4, .4))
row_labels(labels[match(violations, fn)]); yy <- 7:1
panel(c(0, 100), 7, "Party advantage offsets the violation", seq(0, 100, 25),
      xlabel = "Share preferring co-partisan despite violation (%)")
for (k in 1:3) {
  z <- pick(comp_est, paste(c("lib", "mod", "con")[k], violations, sep = "."))
  ci(z, yy + c(.18, 0, -.18)[k], color = cols[k], scale = 100)
}
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
legend("center", c("Liberal", "Moderate", "Conservative"), col = cols, pch = 16,
       bty = "n", cex = .85, horiz = TRUE)
```

Rows are violations and colors ideology groups. Points are bounded estimates and bars 95% log-odds
intervals. All other attributes of the two candidates are equal.

`sc_ratio()` returns $-\tau_j / \tau_p$, the mean prosecution penalty in units of the mean partisan
gain, with a delta-method standard error.

```{r}
#| label: gs-ratio
price <- sc_ratio("journalists penalty / co-partisan gain",
                  sc_mean("journalists, partisans", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", w = "PL"),
                  sc_mean("co-partisan", "diff_respParty", w = "PL"))
tab(sc_estimate(gs, price))
```

The ratio is 1.14 (95% interval 0.91 to 1.37), so on average the two are of similar size.

## Candidate contests

`sc_contest()` estimates the expected share choosing the first candidate in a specified matchup,
with position effects set to zero and task shocks kept. The paper places a co-partisan at each
social-policy position (1 most liberal, 4 most conservative) against a non-co-partisan at position
3, all else equal. The co-partisan has a clean record or prosecutes journalists. The contrast is
the coded difference between the two candidates. The groups are liberal, moderate and conservative
partisans and leaners.

```{r}
#| label: gs-contests
e <- function(f) as.numeric(fn %in% f)
contests <- list()
for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
  d <- e("diff_respParty") + (pos - 3) * e("diff_p2_num")
  if (violation == "journalists") d <- d + e("diff_dem_code_u_journalists")
  contests[[length(contests) + 1]] <- sc_contest(paste(ideo, violation, pos, sep = "."), d,
                                                 w = as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL)
}
contest_est <- sc_estimate(gs, contests)
wide <- matrix(round(100 * contest_est$estimate, 1), ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(paste(rep(c("liberal", "moderate", "conservative"), each = 2),
                                     c("clean", "journalists"), sep = ", "),
                               paste("position", 1:4)))
wide
```

At position 2, the co-partisan who prosecutes journalists receives an estimated 49.8% of support
among liberal partisans and leaners and 52.1% among conservative ones. Without the violation, the
same candidate receives 74.2% and 67.7%, so the violation costs about 24 and 16 points. These
expected vote shares include task shocks, so they differ from the compensation shares.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-contests
#| fig-cap: "Expected support in candidate contests"
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 3.3
paper_par()
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3.2, 3.4, 2.6, .8), oma = c(.7, 0, 0, 0))
for (k in 1:3) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 4), ylim = c(0, 100), xlab = "Social policy position",
       ylab = if (k == 1) "Expected vote share (%)" else "", axes = FALSE)
  abline(h = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100), col = "#E8E8E8"); abline(h = 50, lty = 2, col = "#777777")
  axis(1, at = 1:4); axis(2, at = c(0, 50, 100))
  title(c("Liberal", "Moderate", "Conservative")[k], line = .8, cex.main = 1)
  for (v in c("clean", "journalists")) {
    z <- pick(contest_est, paste(c("lib", "mod", "con")[k], v, 1:4, sep = "."))
    cc <- if (v == "clean") blue else red
    polygon(c(1:4, 4:1), 100 * c(z$lower, rev(z$upper)), col = adjustcolor(cc, .12), border = NA)
    lines(1:4, 100 * z$estimate, col = cc, lwd = 1.5, lty = if (v == "clean") 1 else 2)
    points(1:4, 100 * z$estimate, col = cc, pch = if (v == "clean") 16 else 17, cex = .7)
  }
  if (k == 2) legend("bottomleft", c("No violation", "Prosecutes journalists"), col = c(blue, red),
                     lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n", cex = .75)
}
```

Blue lines have no violation, red dashed lines prosecute journalists. The opponent stays at
position 3. Shading gives pointwise 95% log-odds intervals.

## Attribute importance

`sc_importance()` gives each attribute's share of a respondent's utility variation over a stated
menu of levels. The paper uses seven attributes: party, the two four-point policy scales, the
fifteen governance, violation and scandal codes as one attribute, sex, race and profession. A
policy scale has one column, so its menu is `matrix(1:4)`. The shares sum to one and come from one
joint update, about nine minutes per group. The package gives no intervals for them, because in the
paper's simulations those intervals cover less often than stated. The groups are all partisans and
leaners, Democrats, and Republicans (leaners included).

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance
attrs <- list(party = "diff_respParty", econ = "diff_p1_num", social = "diff_p2_num",
              conduct = grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn, value = TRUE),
              sex = grep("^diff_sex_", fn, value = TRUE),
              race = grep("^diff_race_", fn, value = TRUE),
              profession = grep("^diff_pro_", fn, value = TRUE))
imp_groups <- list(All = "PL", Dem = function(g) g$party == "Dem", Rep = function(g) g$party == "Rep")
imp <- estimate_each(gs, lapply(names(imp_groups), function(k)
  sc_importance(attrs, menus = list(econ = matrix(1:4), social = matrix(1:4)),
                w = imp_groups[[k]], names = paste(k, names(attrs), sep = "."))))
imp[, c("name", "estimate", "plug_in", "n", "status")]
```

The figure groups the components into four: policy (economic and social), party, governance and
conduct, and background (sex, race and profession).

```{r}
#| label: gs-importance-summary
combine <- list(policy = c("econ", "social"), party = "party", governance = "conduct",
                background = c("sex", "race", "profession"))
imp_display <- sapply(names(imp_groups), function(k)
  sapply(combine, function(a) sum(pick(imp, paste(k, a, sep = "."))$estimate)))
round(100 * imp_display, 1)
```

Among all partisans and leaners, policy accounts for 46.5% of utility variation, party for 32.9%,
governance and conduct for 18.3%, and background traits for 2.3%. Policy outweighs party among
Democrats (52.5% against 29.5%). Among Republicans the two are close (39.7% against 36.7%).

```{r}
#| label: fig-gs-importance
#| fig-cap: "Attribute importance by party"
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.1
paper_par()
layout(matrix(1:2, 2), heights = c(3.35, .45))
par(mar = c(3, 9.7, .7, 1.1))
xmax <- max(50, 10 * ceiling((100 * max(imp_display) + 5) / 10))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, xmax), ylim = c(.5, 4.5), axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "Mean importance share (%)", ylab = "")
abline(v = seq(0, xmax, 10), col = "#E8E8E8", lwd = .6)
axis(1, at = seq(0, xmax, 10))
axis(2, at = 4:1, labels = c("Policy", "Party", "Governance/conduct", "Background"),
     tick = FALSE, cex.axis = .95)
imp_cols <- c("#333333", blue, red)
for (k in 1:3) {
  s <- imp_display[, k]
  stopifnot(abs(sum(s) - 1) < 1e-8)
  y <- 4:1 + c(.20, 0, -.20)[k]
  rect(0, y - .075, 100 * s, y + .075, col = imp_cols[k], border = NA)
  text(100 * s, y, sprintf("%.1f", 100 * s), pos = 4, offset = .55, col = imp_cols[k], cex = .78)
}
par(mar = rep(0, 4)); plot.new()
legend("center", c("All partisans and leaners", "Democrat", "Republican"),
       fill = imp_cols, border = NA, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE, cex = .85)
```

The bars are the pooled group (dark grey), Democrats (blue, 723 respondents) and Republicans (red,
654). The shares are point estimates, with equal weights over each attribute's stated levels, and
sum to 100% within each group.

## Decisiveness

`sc_decisiveness()` gives how often exchanging two candidates' levels on one attribute would
reverse the choice, holding the other attributes and the task shock fixed. It averages over the
matchups each respondent saw. The conduct swaps take about twenty minutes.

```{r}
#| label: gs-decisiveness
conduct <- grep("^diff_dem_code_", fn)
action <- grep("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", fn[conduct])
generic <- c(TRUE, grepl("^diff_dem_code_g_", fn[conduct]))   # reference row plus generic codes
dec <- estimate_each(gs, list(
  sc_decisiveness(list(party = "diff_respParty"), pairs = list(party = c(2L, 1L)),
                  names = "party", w = "PL"),
  sc_decisiveness(list(conduct = fn[conduct]), pairs = list(conduct = cbind(1L + action, 1L)),
                  allowed = list(conduct = generic),
                  names = sub("^diff_dem_code_[uv]_", "", fn[conduct][action]))))
tab(dec)
```

Exchanging party reverses an estimated 36.1% of choices among partisans and leaners (95% interval
33.8% to 38.4%). Exchanging a candidate who prosecutes journalists with one at the generic
reference position reverses 32.0% (27.3% to 37.1%), the most of the seven violations.

## All paper targets

`gs_targets()` below builds every GS quantity in the paper's main results file from the public
functions: a mean and a share for each of the 30 features, the compensation shares for seven
violations in three ideology groups, 24 contests, the switch AMEs and the ratio. With bounded
updates for its 51 shares, `sc_estimate(gs, gs_targets(gs))` takes about 40 minutes in one process.
It reproduces the paper's estimates, standard errors and intervals.

```{r}
#| label: gs-full
gs_targets <- function(st) {
  fn <- st$data$data$feature_names; g <- st$data$groups
  e1 <- function(j) as.numeric(seq_along(fn) == j)
  tl <- list(); add <- function(t) tl[[length(tl) + 1L]] <<- t
  for (j in seq_along(fn)) {
    w <- if (j == 1L) "PL" else NULL
    add(sc_mean(paste0(fn[j], ".mean"), fn[j], w)); add(sc_share(paste0(fn[j], ".share"), fn[j], w))
  }
  actions <- grep("^diff_dem_code_u_", fn)
  for (ideo in c("lib", "mod", "con")) {
    wi <- as.numeric(g$ideology == ideo) * g$PL
    for (j in actions) add(sc_share(paste0("comp.", ideo, ".", fn[j]), c(fn[j], fn[1L]), wi))
    for (violation in c("clean", "journalists")) for (pos in 1:4) {
      v <- e1(1L) + (pos - 3) * e1(3L)
      if (violation == "journalists") v <- v + e1(match("diff_dem_code_u_journalists", fn))
      add(sc_contest(paste0("contest.", ideo, ".", violation, ".", pos), v, w = wi))
    }
  }
  jm <- sc_mean("journalists.partisan.mean", "diff_dem_code_u_journalists", "PL"); add(jm)
  for (j in c(1:3, actions, grep("^diff_dem_code_v_", fn))) {
    if (j == 1L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "party", function(k) c(D = 1L, R = 2L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]],
                        function(k) c(D = 2L, R = 1L, I = NA_integer_)[[k]], design = "gs", w = "PL"))
    } else if (j <= 3L) {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), paste0("p", j - 1L), 4L, 1L, design = "gs", scale = 1 / 3))
    } else {
      add(sc_ame_switch(paste0(fn[j], ".ame"), "dem", fn[j], "g_boardElect", design = "gs"))
    }
  }
  add(sc_ratio("journalists.party.price", jm, sc_mean("diff_respParty.mean", "diff_respParty", "PL")))
  tl
}
```

As above, the policy AMEs are per point of the scale.
